sql:
SELECT z.LocationID, z.Borough, z.Zone, COUNT(t.PULocationID) AS cash_trips
FROM ops.zones z
LEFT JOIN lake.trips t ON t.PULocationID = z.LocationID AND t.payment_type = 2
GROUP BY z.LocationID, z.Borough, z.Zone
ORDER BY z.LocationID

diagnosis.bottleneck: The query spends most of its time scanning the large trips table to find payment_type=2 rows (≈99k rows), then hash-joining them with the small zones table (265 rows) and finally hash-aggregating the 99k joined rows. The outer join predicate (including a cast) and the lack of pre-aggregation on the trips side cause unnecessary work.

plan_nodes.note: Join Type: RIGHT | Conditions: CAST(PULocationID AS BIGINT) = LocationID | Estimated Cardinality: 99167

hypotheses.claim: A filter on the joined side sits in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN; the join dominates the cost. (matched: left join lake.trips t on … and t.payment_type = 2)

The hash join probes a 265-row zones hash table with 99,167 filtered trips rows. Pre-aggregating trips by PULocationID (where payment_type=2) before the join would reduce the probe side to at most 243 distinct keys, making the join and subsequent group-by much cheaper.

The join condition uses CAST(PULocationID AS BIGINT) = LocationID, adding a per-row cast overhead and potentially preventing partition-wise join or other join optimizations. Aligning the data types of PULocationID and LocationID would remove the cast.

The sequential scan on trips reads all 495,833 rows to apply the payment_type=2 filter. An index on (payment_type, PULocationID) would allow an index-only scan to fetch only the ~99k relevant rows, reducing I/O.
